title: Best Music Producers (2026): How to Hire One for Your Song
description: How to hire a music producer online: what the package should include, how to brief your song, rights and royalties, price factors and red flags.
intro: A music producer turns a song idea, a voice memo or a rough demo into a finished arrangement: drums, bass, instruments and sound. Online collaborations work well when the brief is clear and the rights are settled in writing. They go wrong when ownership, credits and royalties are left vague until the song is released. This guide covers both the music and the paperwork.

faq.q: Who owns the song after production?
faq.a: It depends on the agreement. Composition rights (melody and lyrics) and the recording itself can be owned separately, and some producers ask for a share of royalties or a credit. Agree on ownership, credits and any royalty split in writing before work starts.

faq.q: Does production include mixing and mastering?
faq.a: Sometimes. Many producers deliver a produced track with a rough mix, and offer mixing and mastering as an extra or leave it to a specialist. Check what the final files will be ready for.

faq.q: What should I send if I only have a voice memo?
faq.a: That can be enough to start. Add the lyrics, the tempo if you know it, and reference tracks that show the sound you want. A clear reference is often more useful than a long description.
Ask for them. Stems are separate audio files for each instrument or group, useful for mixing, remixes, live shows or future edits. Some producers include them only in higher packages.
Ask. Royalty-free sample packs are usually fine for release; samples taken from other recordings need permission. Uncleared samples can get a release taken down.
